result.summary: The Argives hold funeral rites and games for the infant Archemorus, killed by the serpent. After the pyre, a marble tomb and a procession of ancestral images, the games begin with a chariot race, a footrace, discus, boxing, wrestling and archery, and the arrow that flies back foretells that only Adrastus will return from the war.

scenes.title: Rumour and the mourning house
scenes.summary: Rumour announces the games, and the princes arrive at the grieving palace where Adrastus vainly consoles the father.
scenes.stakes: The parents' grief threatens to overwhelm them.

scenes.title: Building the pyre
scenes.summary: The pyre is heaped with rich offerings and an ancient grove is felled; the bier is carried out with Hypsipyle among the mourners.
scenes.stakes: Ancient woods and sacred things are destroyed to appease the dead.

scenes.title: Eurydice's lament and the burning
scenes.summary: Eurydice blames Hypsipyle and demands her death. Lycurgus burns his sceptre and hair, the pyre is burned and purified, and a marble tomb rises.
scenes.stakes: Hypsipyle faces the grieving mother's demand for her death.

scenes.title: The crowd and ancestral images
scenes.summary: A great crowd gathers in a valley, and images of ancestral heroes are paraded.

scenes.title: The chariot race
scenes.summary: Apollo watches from Parnassus as Arion bolts and Polynices is thrown. Apollo sends a phantom and Amphiaraus wins.
scenes.stakes: Amphiaraus and Polynices risk injury in the race.

scenes.title: Prizes and the footrace
scenes.summary: Prizes are awarded. Idas cheats Parthenopaeus by seizing his hair, but a rerun is ordered and Parthenopaeus wins after praying to Diana.
scenes.stakes: Parthenopaeus risks shame and civil strife among the Arcadians.

scenes.title: The discus
scenes.summary: Hippomedon's mighty throw outdoes Phlegyas and Menestheus. Adrastus gives prizes and calls for boxing.

scenes.title: Boxing: Capaneus and Alcidamas
scenes.summary: Alcidamas wounds Capaneus with skill. The enraged Capaneus is dragged away.
scenes.stakes: Alcidamas risks being beaten to death by Capaneus.

scenes.title: Wrestling: Tydeus and Agylleus
scenes.summary: Tydeus defeats the giant Agylleus by lifting him as Hercules did Antaeus.
scenes.stakes: Tydeus risks defeat by a much larger foe.

scenes.title: Adrastus's arrow
scenes.summary: Adrastus stops a sword duel and shoots an arrow that returns to his quiver, an omen that he alone will survive the war.
scenes.stakes: The Argive host's fate is foreshadowed as doomed.

alias_notes.explanation: Roman title of Diana at crossroads.

notable_quotes.reason: Reflection that people ignore omens and then blame Fortune.
The returning arrow foreshadows Adrastus as sole survivor.

analysis.text: Funeral games turn grief into competition, while omens like the thrown Polynices and the returning arrow foreshadow the coming war's doom.
The games echo Greek funeral games and the Nemean festival, whose founding was tied to Archemorus.

legacy.text: The episode is the mythic origin of the Nemean Games, and its funeral games follow the model of Homer's Iliad Book 23 and Virgil's Aeneid Book 5.

fun_facts.text: Statius's games closely imitate Virgil's funeral games for Anchises in Aeneid 5, and Homer's for Patroclus.

language_notes.text: Danaan and Inachidae both mean Argives (Greeks of Argos); Inachidae are 'descendants of Inachus', the river-god and legendary first king of Argos.
Lists the great games: Olympic (Alcides, i.e. Hercules, against Pelops at Pisa), Pythian (Apollo's victory over the Python), and Isthmian (for Palaemon).
The 'consort of Tithonus' is Dawn; her 'toil-bringing car' is the sunrise chariot that wakes men to work.
Night and Sleep with 'empty horn' means Sleep's horn of dreams or poppy-juice is spent as dawn drives them off.
Pelasgians here simply means Greeks; the princes feel they are blamed for the child's death and weep to plead innocence.
Compares the king's deafness to comfort with the sea and lightning ignoring pleas and frail clouds: all are beyond persuasion.
Linus was a child of Argos killed by dogs, the story woven on the coverlet; it echoes the dead boy's fate by serpent.
'Seen Nymphs pass and yet be living' means the grove is older than the age when nymphs and fauns were thought to roam.
Niobe's twelve children were slain by Apollo and Diana ('the quivers twain'); she was later linked with Mount Sipylus.
"Argive matrons": Argos stands for the Greek army generally; the women are those of the Greek host marching against Thebes.
"Cadmus" founded Thebes; "Tyrian" refers to his Phoenician origin from Tyre. Eurydice says Thebes has not yet suffered any loss in this war.
"Ogyian" means Theban, from Ogyges, an ancient legendary king associated with Thebes.
The "Thunderer" is Jupiter; Lycurgus's sceptre bears his emblems as the priest of Jupiter. He offers his hair to the god as a vow.
"Mulciber" is a name for Vulcan, god of fire, used here by metonymy for the fire itself.
"Lucifer" here is the morning star, the planet Venus as herald of dawn, not the later Christian devil.
Ephyre is an old name for Corinth, site of the Isthmian games; the circus of Oenomaus was at Pisa, near Olympia. Both are famous venues of crowds.
The Tirynthian is Hercules, raised at Tiryns; the lion is the Nemean lion, strangled in his first labour.
Inachidae means descendants of Inachus, that is the Argives, who are watching the games.
Io was turned into a heifer by Jupiter and guarded by hundred-eyed Argus, whose eyes sleep in turns, hence 'know no setting'.
Tantalus is distinguished from his punished namesake in the underworld; here he is shown as the gods' guest before his offence.
Pelops won Hippodamia by a chariot race with horses given by Neptune; Myrtilos, his rival's charioteer, was later betrayed and killed by him.
Danaus and Aegyptus were brothers; Danaus's daughters killed Aegyptus's sons on their wedding night, hence 'the coming night'.
Phoebus is Apollo, god of song and prophecy, invoked here as the poet's Muse-like inspirer.
Amphitryon's son is Hercules, who served Eurystheus and performed the Labours; Arion is said to have carried him in war.
Refers to Phaethon, son of the Sun, who lost control of his father's chariot and was destroyed; Adrastus' warning parallels this.
Cyllarus was Castor's horse; the Oebalian (Spartan) steeds are said to be its offspring, begotten while Castor was away with the Argonauts.
Thoas and Euneos are Hypsipyle's sons by Jason; Euneos' name recalls the good omen of the Argo's voyage.
Apollo's songs recall Jove's battle with the Giants at Phlegra and Apollo's killing of the Python (the serpent).
Apollo served Admetus as a herdsman after being punished by Jove; Admetus treated him with respect.
The thread and distaff refer to the Fates spinning each life's thread; Amphiaraus' life is nearly spun out.
Tyrrhenian blast means the Etruscan trumpet, here the signal to start the race.
Pelasgi: an old name for the Greeks, used here for the Argive spectators.
Olenian horns: the horns of the constellation Capella (the Goat), linked with Olenus and associated with rain and storms.
Sons of Inachus: the Argives, named for Inachus, Argos' river-god and early king.
Thessalian Admetus: king of Pherae in Thessaly, whose horses were famous.
Oeclides: Amphiaraus, son of Oecles. The 'seer of Phoebus' is the same man.
Son of Labdacus: Polynices, Theban descendant of Labdacus, grandfather of Oedipus.
That awful hunger: Hippodamus' Thracian horses were bred like the man-eating mares of Diomedes, which Hercules overcame; Chromis, a son of Hercules, saves him.
Guardian of dusky Lethe: probably Cerberus, hound of the underworld. Eumenides are the Furies.
Aonian exile: Polynices, a Theban (Aonia is Boeotia) banished from his city.
Tisiphone, a Fury, preserves Polynices so that the war between the brothers may proceed.
Archemorus: the infant whose death began the funeral games; his funeral was lavish.
Ocean-sire: Arion's father Neptune, god of the sea and of horses.
The Tirynthian is Hercules, who was associated with Tiryns in Argolis. The bowl once belonged to him.
The scene shows the battle of Lapithae and Centaurs, where Hercules fought the Centaur Hylaeus.
Phrixean waters are the Hellespont, named for Phrixus, whose sister Helle fell from the golden ram there. The swimmer is Leander.
The Sestian maid is Hero of Sestos, who watched from her tower for Leander swimming to her; her lamp guided him.
Olympian wreaths: Idas won at the Olympic games, held at Pisa in Elis.
The draughts of Pallas means olive oil, Minerva's (Pallas') gift, rubbed on athletes' skin.
Cydonian means from Cydonia in Crete, whose archers were famous.
Trivia is Diana. The Ogygian war is the war against Thebes, whose legendary founder was Ogyges.
Quoit: the discus, here a heavy bronze disk thrown for distance.
Sons of Inachus: the Argives, named for Inachus, the legendary first king and river-god of Argos.
Ephyre is Corinth; Pisa is the district of Olympia; Acarnania lies in western Greece. The list shows contestants from across the Greek world.
Tyrian towers: Thebes, whose founder Cadmus came from Tyre. The Argive army is marching against it.
Bistonian plain and Mount Pangaeus are in Thrace, homeland of Mars, god of war.
Alpheos is the river at Olympia, site of the great festival and games Phlegyas attended.
The eclipsed moon: Thessalian witches were believed to draw the moon down by spells, while people clashed bronze to rescue her.
Son of Maia is Mercury, god of athletes and patron of the palaestra.
Polyphemus, the Cyclops blinded by Ulixes (Ulysses), hurled rocks at the escaping ship, guided only by sound.
The Aloidae, giant brothers, piled Ossa and Pelion on Olympus to storm heaven.
Gnosian: from Gnossus (Cnossos) in Crete, famous for archers and bows.
Cestus: the boxer's glove of leather thongs, often weighted with metal.
Aonian means Theban, from Aonia in Boeotia. Capaneus wishes to fight an enemy rather than a kinsman.
Laconians: people of Laconia, the region around Sparta. Dorian princes here means Greek leaders, and Alcidamas is a Spartan.
Pollux, divine twin of Castor, was a famed boxer and son of Jove by Leda; as a Spartan hero he trains Alcidamas.
Tityos was a giant punished in the underworld, where vultures ate his liver. Capaneus is compared to him in size.
Gloves: boxers wore leather thongs or gloves (caestus), often weighted, so they are 'dulled' by mere rubbing.
'Enters his guard and overshadows him' means Alcidamas steps inside Capaneus's defence and, rising above, attacks from higher.
Cowhide: the leather of the boxing gloves, which Capaneus sees stained with blood.
Oebalian means Spartan, from Oebalus, a legendary Spartan king. Capaneus insults Alcidamas as an 'eunuch-boy' kept for favours.
Taygetus is the mountain range beside Sparta, so 'nursling of Taygetus' means Alcidamas was raised in Sparta.
The Aetolian is Tydeus, who comes from Aetolia in Greece. His covering of boar-hide recalls his father's land and the famous Calydonian boar.
Cleonaean means from Cleonae, near Nemea. It links Agylleus to Hercules, whose first labour was the Nemean lion; hence the comparison of size.
Oenides means 'son of Oeneus', a patronymic naming Tydeus.
'Clad themselves in showers of sand': wrestlers threw sand over their oiled bodies to get a grip.
Iberian refers to Spain, famed in antiquity for its mines.
The earth-born Libyan is Antaeus, a giant who drew strength from his mother Earth. Hercules defeated him by lifting him off the ground.
The double negative 'held not no small measure' is a rhetorical question: Tydeus says the plain of Dirce did hold much of his blood.
The Dircaean exile is a Theban, named for Dirce, a spring near Thebes; probably Polynices' follower. Not yet doomed means he will die later in the war.
"Great store of death remains" means plenty of killing still lies ahead in the war, so they should save their fury for the enemy.
Adrastus's son-in-law is Polynices, who is hailed as victor of Thebes, the city he hopes to win; the Fates answer ominously because he will not.
Lyctian means from Lyctus in Crete, a place famed for its archers and bows.
The circus here is the open running-ground of the funeral games; its length is the range for the shot.
"Well-known quiver" means the arrow returns to the quiver it came from, as if it knew its home.

context_notes.text: The father is Lycurgus, priest of Jove at Nemea, whose infant son Opheltes (Archemorus) was killed by a serpent.
Adrastus is king of Argos, leader of the expedition against Thebes, and host of the princes.
Cypress was a funeral tree, and spices like incense and cinnamon were burned on rich pyres.
The augur, probably Amphiaraus, advises funeral rites to atone for the serpent's death, an ill omen for the war.
Hypsipyle, former queen of Lemnos, was the child's nurse and had left him unguarded when the serpent came; her own sons have just found her.
Eurydice is the mother of the dead infant Opheltes (Archemorus), who was left by his nurse Hypsipyle to show the Greek army a spring.
Circling the pyre with reversed arms was a Roman-style military funeral rite, here applied to the Greek kings honouring the child.
Mavors is Mars, god of war. His uncertain hovering foreshadows the coming Theban conflict.
The bulls and cows are to be sacrificed at the funeral rites for Opheltes, for which the games are held.
Parading ancestral images was a Roman funeral custom, here applied to the Argive heroes' forebears.
Acrisius was Danaë's father, who shut her away; Perseus, her son by Jupiter, later killed him accidentally.
Arion was a famous divine horse, offspring of Neptune, later owned by Adrastus, king of Argos.
Parnassus was the mountain sacred to Apollo and the Muses.
Lots were drawn to assign each chariot its starting position.
Arion is the divine horse driven by Polynices in this race; he was once Adrastus' horse, and he fears the new driver.
Phoebus (Apollo) was Amphiaraus' patron as a seer; Amphiaraus is fated to die in the coming war.
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld, from which the phantom may have come.
Atalanta, Parthenopaeus' mother, was a huntress who raced her suitors and defeated them until Hippomenes tricked her with golden apples.
Idas grabs the hair Parthenopaeus had vowed to Diana, which is why the prayer to her follows.
The son of Talaus is Adrastus, king of Argos, who presides over the funeral games.
Capaneus is the arrogant, impious Argive warrior who scorns the gods; he is eager to fight.
Adrastus, king of Argos, hosts the funeral games for Opheltes and keeps order among the Argive leaders.
Tydeus and Hippomedon are fellow Argive champions in the expedition against Thebes, so they are able to restrain Capaneus.
The Achelous is a major river in Aetolia, Tydeus' homeland.
Dirce is a spring and river near Thebes. Tydeus was wounded there while serving as envoy, when he fought off an ambush by the Thebans.
Adrastus, king of Argos and son of Iasus, leads the Seven against Thebes. He is stopping a duel in the funeral games for Archemorus.
A golden helm is the consolation prize, given so neither duelist is dishonoured by the interrupted fight.
Adrastus is the only one of the seven leaders to return home alive from the war, as the myth tells.

literary_notes.text: The princes' sporting rivalry is likened to ships trying out their gear on a calm lake before braving the sea, like war after games.
The mother's frenzied grief, greater than the father's, is shown through her actions and her urging of the maidens.
Warlike spoils burned for an infant stress the contrast between the great honours and the small life lost.
The narrator breaks in with an exclamation on 'insatiable hopes', pitying the mother's now-futile preparations.
The ancient tree is said to rise above the stars and outlive Nymphs and Fauns, stressing its sanctity before its fall.
Pales, Silvanus and the Nymphs weep and cling to the trees, making the felling of the forest a human tragedy.
The felling is compared to soldiers sacking a captured city, so vanishing swiftly that the grove is like a conquered town.
Eurydice asks who is to blame, voicing her bewildered grief and her sense that the gods are hostile to her family.
Calling Hypsipyle "the fiend" shows how grief twists Eurydice's judgment; she resents the nurse's closeness to her child.
The bereaved cow searching the fields compares Eurydice's grief to animal mourning, making her sorrow raw and elemental.
The extravagant list of melting jewels, silver and gold stresses the pyre's unmatched splendour and the scale of the mourning.
The description of the sculpted tomb retells the child's story in art, ending with a vivid image of the serpent that seems alive.
Rumour is pictured as a herald actively summoning the crowds, showing how swiftly news spreads.
The warriors' glad confidence in their numbers is ironic given the disastrous war against Thebes that awaits them.
The contrast with the Tantalus of the underworld evokes his later punishment while praising this earlier, pious image.
The false peace of Danaus hints at the coming slaughter of the wedding night, a hidden menace among the ancestral images.
The horses are compared to flocks of birds racing and winds contesting under Aeolus, stressing their speed and wildness.
The Phaethon comparison and the cruel Fates hint that Polynices, driving Arion, will fail to heed warnings and be thrown.
Apollo speaks directly to Amphiaraus, who cannot hear, heightening the pathos of his coming death.
A string of comparisons to ships, javelins, clouds and torrents exaggerates the speed of the start.
The lash's strokes are compared to hail and rain, conveying their density and violence.
The frightened Polynices is likened to a helpless steersman, suggesting that his skill has failed and chance rules.
The race is said to be harsher than war, stressing the competitors' fury.
Ships held motionless between tide and wind picture Chromis and Hippodamus locked together, struggling in vain.
The narrator turns to address Amphiaraus directly, adding solemnity and sympathy for the doomed seer.
The narrator calls Polynices' survival untimely, since his death would have spared the war that follows.
The glory goes to the horse while the prize goes to the prophet, a neat division.
The embroidered swimmer is so lifelike that one would expect wet hair, praising the artist's skill.
Parthenopaeus is compared to Hesperus, the evening star, outshining others and reflected in the sea, to stress his unmatched beauty.
The runners are likened to stags fleeing a lion, conveying their panic and speed.
Even his tears become a beauty, showing the poet's persistent focus on the boy's looks.
He runs so lightly that he leaves no mark in the dust, showing the goddess's answer to his prayer.
The disk's glare is compared to the shield of Mars, conveying its terrifying size and brightness.
The plummeting disk is compared to the moon falling in eclipse, giving the throw cosmic scale.
Fortune is imagined as an agent who takes pleasure in crushing overconfident hopes.
Hippomedon's throw is likened to Polyphemus hurling the rock, lending it mythic grandeur.
Capaneus's grim look and bloodthirsty challenge reveal his violent, boastful nature.
Capaneus is likened to the giant Tityos rising from the Underworld, stressing his monstrous size against the youthful Alcidamas.
Water breaking against a rock pictures Alcidamas's fluid evasions as Capaneus's force spends itself and falls back.
Capaneus's rage is compared to a wounded lion or tiger, showing his bestial fury once he sees blood.
The rowers' brief rest and recall to the oars mirror the fighters' pause before they fight again.
Capaneus's slurs and wish to smash the boy reveal his arrogance, cruelty and refusal to accept defeat.
Tydeus' small body housing great fury is a trait of his character throughout the epic.
The cypress bending to the south wind and springing back compares the tall Agylleus bending over Tydeus.
Fighting bulls, boars and bears elevate the wrestling to a primal struggle. The heifer's presence adds a note of rivalry and desire.
The buried miner suggests the crushing fall of Agylleus' bulk, adding a grim touch of mortality to a sporting scene.
The comparison to Hercules and Antaeus gives Tydeus heroic stature and explains his lift. It also reverses the earlier Hercules comparison, which applied to Agylleus' size.
The Fates echoing the proclamation darkly hints that Polynices will never be victor of Thebes.
The narrator steps out to moralize that people ignore clear omens and then blame Fortune for the consequences.
The arrow flying back to its quiver is a portent, a strange event that foretells Adrastus alone coming home.
The narrator openly explains the omen, telling us that only Adrastus will survive the war and return in sorrow.
